body_markdown:
Who couldn’t love the E-Type? It was unforgettable, it had a long, long run and, right up to the present day, many, many admirers. Its styling, upon introduction in 1961, was not only show-car advanced, but the shape still says “Jaguar” to most anyone.


Jaguar


The final E-Types offered lots to talk about, for the 4.2-liter six was out and the 5.3-liter V-12,[originally introduced in the XJ sedans](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1974-jaguar-xj12l-low-lean-luxurious/) , now rode under the hood. Roadsters now had the same long wheelbase as the outgoing 4.2 2+2 coupes, giving the open cars a much slinkier look—arguably the prettiest of the 1961–75 convertibles, proportion-wise.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The new V-12s made 272 horsepower at 5850 rpm and 304 lb-ft at 3600 rpm—DIN figures in both cases. Wheels were also wider in V-12 cars, six inches instead of five. With both convertible and coupe riding the same 105-inch wheelbase, total length was now 186 inches, per the 1973 U.S. brochure.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The V-12s first appeared in 1971 and sported standard pressed-steel wheels with trim rings and hub caps. The long-standing chromed wire wheels were still available, but now an option.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Transmission choices were the long-standing four-speed manual or an optional three-speed BorgWarner automatic. Only the 2+2 coupe was available, the two-seat coupe having been discontinued with the introduction of the V-12 models.


Thomas Klockau


U.S. versions, with their added emissions equipment, air pump, and the like, were slightly less lively than their home-market counterparts—but only a bit. Per the ’73 brochure, SAE figures were 241 hp at 5750 rpm with 285 lb-ft at 3500 rpm, both solid figures good for the time.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As the brochure told prospects: “A new breed of power! The V-12 engine propels the car from 0 to 60 in 6.8 seconds. Top speed is almost a fifth of the speed of sound. Yet, its amazing quickness is almost surpassed by its supreme smoothness.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“That’s because our 5.3 litres of capacity are spread over twelve cylinders. Since the cylinders and pistons are smaller, the crankshaft receives a smaller pulse with each power stroke, but these pulses arrive with more frequency.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“Result: smoothness. A whispering turbine-like smoothness through the entire range of driving speeds.” Fuel economy? Er, never mind. But hey! This was a Jaguar, not a Vega, Corolla, or Pinto Squire…


Jaguar


The 2+2 was discontinued by autumn of ’74, with only the convertible left to carry the torch. Jaguar was already knee-deep in developing the E’s successor, the XJS. Sure, the E-Type was unmistakable and timeless, but by 1974–75, the basic design was rather long in the tooth, and there were limits to the sprucing up, to the addition of new technology and gadgets, and to the modern HVAC systems fitted in the aging chassis.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The convertible’s production ended not much later than that of the 2+2 coupe, and the final 50 cars, all finished in black (except for a single unit, painted dark green for a special customer), received a dash plaque attesting to their being the last of their kind.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


All told, 72,507 E-Types of all sorts were made between 1961 and 1975. Of those, 7990 were V-12 convertibles, and 7297 were V-12 2+2 coupes. Today’s Azure Blue example ([one of 12 available colors](http://lov2xlr8.no/brochures/1970/73e/bilder/10.jpg) ), with a lovely contrasting saddle tan interior, is one of 5182 left-hand-drive models built.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Your author spotted it at a show at Eriksen Chevrolet in Milan, Illinois, back on August 30. It was one of the first cars I saw as I approached from the parking lot, and I was immediately smitten. It was in amazing overall shape, and I loved the color combination.


Thomas Klockau
